title: Ὄνον ἀγοράζων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 263. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνον τις ἀγοράσαι μέλλων ἐπὶ πείρᾳ αὐτὸν ἔλαβε· καὶ εἰσαγαγὼν εἰς τοὺς ἰδίους ἐπὶ τῆς φάτνης αὐτὸν ἔστησεν.
sentences.tr: Onon tis agorasai mellōn epi peirāi auton elabe· kai eisagagōn eis tous idious epi tēs phatnēs auton estēsen.
sentences.l: Someone being about to buy a donkey took him on trial; and having brought him in among his own he set him at the manger.
sentences.i: A man who meant to buy a donkey took him on trial, brought him in among his own beasts and set him at the manger.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ πείρᾳ, 'on trial' — the sale is conditional and the animal returnable, which is what the whole fable hangs on. τοὺς ἰδίους, 'his own', leaves the noun unexpressed: his own donkeys, supplied from the sense.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ καταλιπὼν τοὺς ἄλλους παρὰ τῷ ἀργοτάτῳ καὶ ἀδηφάγῳ ἔστη.
sentences.tr: Ho de katalipōn tous allous para tōi argotatōi kai adēphagōi estē.
sentences.l: But he, having left the others, took his stand beside the idlest and gluttonous one.
sentences.i: But he left the others and planted himself beside the laziest of them, who was a glutton besides.
sentences.n: A single article governs both adjectives, so this is one donkey and not two — the idlest of them, and a glutton besides. ἀργός is α-privative on ἔργον, 'not working'; ἀδηφάγος is 'eating to the full'.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν ἐποίει, δήσας καὶ ἀπαγαγὼν τῷ δεσπότῃ αὐτὸν ἀπέδωκε.
sentences.tr: Kai hōs ouden epoiei, dēsas kai apagagōn tōi despotēi auton apedōke.
sentences.l: And as he was doing nothing, having tied him and led him away he gave him back to his master.
sentences.i: And since the donkey did nothing, he haltered him, led him off and gave him back to his owner.
sentences.n: The imperfect ἐποίει leaves the donkey standing there doing nothing further, while the subject of the participles shifts back to the buyer with no word marking the change — Greek relies on sense to sort out who is doing what.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ διερωτῶντος εἰ οὕτως ἀξίαν αὐτοῦ τὴν δοκιμασίαν ἐποιήσατο, ὑποτυχὼν εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐδὲν ἐπιδέομαι πείρας· οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι τοιοῦτός ἐστιν ὁποῖον ἐξ ἁπάντων τὸν συνήθη ἐπελέξατο. »
sentences.tr: Tou de dierōtōntos ei houtōs axian autou tēn dokimasian epoiēsato, hypotychōn eipen· « All’ egōge ouden epideomai peiras· oida gar hoti toioutos estin hopoion ex hapantōn ton synēthē epelexato. »
sentences.l: And he asking closely whether he had thus made a testing worthy of him, taking-up-the-word he said: « Well, I for my part need no trial at all; for I know that he is such as the one he picked out for himself as his companion from among them all. »
sentences.i: When the owner pressed him whether he had really made a trial worthy of the beast in that way, he answered: « Why, I need no trial at all; I know he is just such as the one he chose for company out of the whole lot. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute carries the owner's questioning; διερωτάω is to ask right through a matter, to press. ὑποτυχών is to take up the word and answer, never a physical seizing — the corpus renders it 'taking-up-the-word'. τοιοῦτος … ὁποῖον is a correlative pair, and Greek says it twice where English says it once.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοιοῦτος εἶναί τις ὑπολαμβάνεται ὁποίοις ἂν ἥδηται τοῖς ἑταίροις.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti toioutos einai tis hypolambanetai hopoiois an hēdētai tois hetairois.
sentences.l: The story shows that a man is supposed to be such as are the companions in whom he takes delight.
sentences.n: ὁποίοις τοῖς ἑταίροις stands in the dative because ἥδομαι, 'take pleasure in', governs a dative in its own clause; the correlative takes the case its own clause requires rather than the nominative of the τοιοῦτος it answers. ἄν with the subjunctive makes the moral a standing rule rather than a report of one case.
